In our family, the smell of simmering vinegar and garlic means one thing: Sunday dinner is coming. Chicken adobo is the dish my grandmother made for every birthday, homecoming, and rainy afternoon, and she never wrote it down. I learned it standing beside her stove, watching her pour soy sauce and vinegar with a confident, unmeasured hand.

Adobo is the unofficial national dish of the Philippines, and every household has its own version. Ours is simple: bone-in chicken thighs, plenty of garlic, whole peppercorns, bay leaves, and a balance of salty and tangy that gets deeper as it cooks. We brown the chicken for richness, then let it braise until tender and glossy.

Serve it over white rice, with sauce spooned on top. It tastes even better the next day, if there are any leftovers. This is the recipe I've pieced together from memory, and I'm honored to share it.

My grandmother made it every Sunday, and the smell of simmering vinegar, soy sauce, garlic, and bay leaves would drift down the street long before we reached her door. She never measured anything. A splash of this, a handful of that, and an insistence that patience was the secret ingredient.

Adobo is called the unofficial national dish of the Philippines, and every household claims its own version. Ours is tangy, savory, and a little sweet, with chicken that turns tender enough to fall off the bone and a glossy sauce made for spooning over steaming white rice.

Sunlight looks white, but it's actually a mix of every color, like a rainbow packed together. You can see those colors when sunlight shines through a prism or when rain makes a rainbow.

Now, Earth is wrapped in a blanket of air called the atmosphere. Air is made of tiny gas molecules, mostly nitrogen and oxygen. When sunlight zooms into the atmosphere, it bumps into these molecules and gets bounced around in all directions. Scientists call this *scattering*.

Here's the cool part: different colors scatter by different amounts. Light travels in waves, and each color has its own wavelength. Red light has long, lazy waves, while blue light has short, quick waves. The tiny air molecules are much better at scattering those short blue waves. So blue light gets tossed all across the sky, and no matter where you look, some of it is heading straight into your eyes.

You might wonder, why isn't the sky purple? Violet light actually scatters even more, but the sun gives off less of it, some gets absorbed high up in the atmosphere, and our eyes aren't very sensitive to violet. Blue wins!

At sunset, sunlight travels through much more air to reach you. Most of the blue gets scattered away, leaving the glowing reds and oranges.

Here is the key part: short waves scatter much more than long waves. Blue light gets bounced around about ten times more than red light.

So when you look up, blue light from the sun has been knocked all over the sky and is coming at your eyes from every direction. That makes the whole sky look blue.

A browser cache is like a short-term memory for your web browser. When you visit a website, your browser downloads many files: images, logos, stylesheets (which control how a page looks), and JavaScript (which makes pages interactive). Downloading all of these takes time, so the browser saves copies on your computer.

The next time you visit the same site, the browser checks its cache first. If it already has a file, it can load it instantly from your device instead of downloading it again. This makes pages load faster and uses less internet data.

But what if a file changes on the website? Websites send instructions along with each file, called headers, that tell the browser how long to keep it. For example, a logo might be cached for a month, while a news headline might be cached for only a few minutes. When the time expires, the browser asks the server whether the file has changed. If not, the server says "keep using your copy," and no re-download is needed. If it has changed, the browser fetches the new version.

Sometimes a cache causes problems, such as showing an outdated version of a page. In that case, you can do a "hard refresh" (often Ctrl+Shift+R or Cmd+Shift+R) or clear your cache in the browser settings to force fresh downloads.

A browser cache is like a small storage box on your computer where your web browser keeps copies of files from websites you visit.

When you open a page for the first time, your browser downloads everything it needs: text, images, style sheets, and scripts. Instead of throwing these files away afterward, it saves many of them in the cache.

The next time you visit that page, the browser checks the cache first. If it already has a file, it can load it from your own device instead of downloading it again. This is much faster, and it saves internet data too.

Of course, websites change. To handle this, servers send instructions with each file, such as how long it can be stored. This is called an expiration time. Once a file is too old, the browser asks the server whether a newer version exists. If nothing has changed, the server says so, and the browser keeps using its saved copy. If the file has changed, the browser downloads the new one and replaces the old copy.

Sometimes a cache causes problems. You might see an outdated version of a page. Refreshing the page with a hard reload (often Ctrl+Shift+R) or clearing your cache in the browser settings forces fresh downloads.

In short, caching helps websites load faster by reusing files you already have.

One year ago, I went from writing code to managing the people who write it. Here's what I've learned:

**1. Your output is now your team's output.** I kept trying to "help" by taking on tickets. It felt productive, but it left me no time for what only I could do: clearing blockers, setting priorities, and giving feedback.

**2. Listening beats fixing.** In 1:1s, I used to jump straight to solutions. Now I ask, "What would you do?" The answers are usually better than mine.

**3. Feedback delayed is feedback denied.** Awkward conversations don't improve with age. Small, timely, specific comments beat a polished review in December.

**4. Clarity is kindness.** Most team friction I've seen came from unclear expectations, not bad intent.

**5. You will miss the code.** And that's okay. The satisfaction now comes from watching someone else ship something they were nervous about.

I'm still learning, and I've made plenty of mistakes along the way.

One year ago I traded my IDE for a calendar. Here is what the first year as an engineering manager taught me.

**1. Your output is your team's output.** I kept measuring my day by what I shipped. The better question is what my team shipped and what blocked them.

**2. Feedback delayed is feedback denied.** Every time I waited for the "right moment," the moment got harder. Small, frequent, specific feedback beats a big review.

**3. Listen first.** Most of my early "fixes" solved the wrong problem. Asking one more question usually saved a week of work.

**4. Protect focus time.** Meetings are easy to add and hard to remove. Guard your team's calendar like you guard production.

**5. Say "I don't know."** It builds more trust than any confident guess.

**6. Career conversations matter.** People rarely ask for growth, but they all want it.

I still miss writing code sometimes. But watching someone on my team land a promotion feels even better than a clean deploy.

**Pride and Prejudice** by Jane Austen (1813)

**Plot:** In rural England, the Bennet family faces a pressing problem: with no male heir, their estate will pass to a distant cousin, so the five daughters need advantageous marriages. When wealthy Mr. Bingley rents a nearby estate, he quickly falls for the eldest daughter, Jane. His friend, the aristocratic Mr. Darcy, seems arrogant and slights the spirited Elizabeth Bennet at a ball. Elizabeth's dislike deepens when the charming officer Mr. Wickham tells her Darcy cruelly cheated him. Meanwhile, Darcy, despite himself, falls in love with her. His first proposal is insulting, emphasizing her inferior family, and Elizabeth rejects him. Darcy then writes her a letter revealing Wickham's true, scandalous character. When Wickham elopes with Elizabeth's youngest sister, Lydia, Darcy quietly intervenes to save the family's reputation. Humbled and transformed, Darcy proposes again, and Elizabeth, having overcome her own misjudgments, accepts. Jane and Bingley also marry.

**Themes:** The novel explores how first impressions and social prejudice distort judgment, and how self-knowledge allows growth. It examines class, showing how rank and wealth shape opportunity, and critiques a society in which marriage is economic necessity for women. Ultimately, Austen champions marriages based on mutual respect, moral character, and affection over mere status or money.

**Pride and Prejudice** by Jane Austen (1813)

**Plot:** In rural England, Mrs. Bennet is determined to marry off her five daughters. When the wealthy Mr. Bingley rents a nearby estate, he quickly takes an interest in the eldest, Jane. His friend, the proud Mr. Darcy, insults the spirited Elizabeth Bennet at a ball, and she forms a lasting dislike of him. Her opinion worsens when the charming officer Mr. Wickham claims Darcy cheated him, and when she learns Darcy encouraged Bingley to abandon Jane. Darcy then surprises Elizabeth with a proposal that is as insulting as it is sincere. She refuses him. In a long letter, he reveals Wickham's true character and explains his own actions. When Wickham elopes with Elizabeth's youngest sister, Lydia, Darcy quietly resolves the scandal. Humbled and changed, both Darcy and Elizabeth come to understand each other, and they finally unite, as do Jane and Bingley.

**Themes:** The novel explores how pride and first impressions cloud judgment, and how self-knowledge allows growth. It examines marriage, money, and class, contrasting unions built on security with those built on genuine respect and affection. Austen also gently satirizes social convention and the limited options available to women of her time.

# Your Notes, Now Synced Even When You're Offline

We've got good news for anyone who has ever jotted down an idea on a plane, in a subway tunnel, or in a café with unreliable Wi-Fi: offline edits now sync automatically.

## What's new

Edit your notes anywhere, with or without a connection. The moment your device reconnects, your changes upload in the background and appear on all your other devices. No manual refresh, no "sync now" button, no lost work.

## How it works

- **Write freely.** Create, edit, and delete notes offline just as you would online.
- **Sync automatically.** When you're back online, changes merge across your devices within seconds.
- **Resolve conflicts smartly.** If you edited the same note on two devices, we keep both versions side by side so nothing gets overwritten.

## Why we built it

Great ideas don't wait for a signal. You told us that losing edits or seeing outdated notes was your biggest frustration, and we listened.

## How to get it

Offline sync is rolling out today to all users. Update to the latest version on iOS, Android, or desktop, and it will turn on automatically.

Questions or feedback? Reach out anytime. Happy note-taking!

**Product Update: Offline Edits Now Sync Automatically**

We have some good news for anyone who has ever lost a thought to a spotty connection. Starting today, your notes sync even when you edit them offline.

**What's new**

Write on a plane, in a subway tunnel, or at a cabin with no signal. Your changes are saved safely on your device. The moment you reconnect, the app uploads those edits and updates every other device you use. There is nothing to tap and nothing to remember.

**How it works**

Each edit is stored locally with a timestamp. When your connection returns, the app merges changes line by line, so edits made on your phone and laptop at different times combine cleanly. If two people change the exact same sentence, we keep both versions and let you choose which one stays.

**What you need to do**

Update to the latest version on iOS, Android, or desktop. Offline sync is turned on by default for all accounts, including free ones.

**Why we built it**

You told us that good ideas rarely wait for Wi-Fi. Many of you asked for a note-taking tool you could trust anywhere, and we heard you.

Happy writing, wherever you are.

**1/5**
Hot take: the best code you'll ever write is the code a tired teammate can understand at 2am during an outage.

Clever code impresses people. Simple code helps them. Only one of those scales. 🧵

**2/5**
Code is read 10x more than it's written.

That one-liner with nested ternaries and a regex might feel like a win today. In six months, it's a puzzle that you (or someone else) has to solve before changing anything.

Optimize for the reader, not the writer.

**3/5**
Clever code hides bugs.

When logic is dense, edge cases blend into the cleverness. Simple code makes wrong behavior *look* wrong.

If a reviewer can't tell whether it's correct at a glance, that's a risk, not a flex.

**4/5**
Simple code is easier to:
✅ Debug
✅ Test
✅ Review
✅ Onboard new people onto
✅ Delete or change when requirements shift

And requirements *always* shift. Flexibility comes from clarity, not from abstractions built for problems you don't have yet.

**5/5**
Rule of thumb: if you have to explain how it works, try rewriting it first.

Save the cleverness for the rare spots where performance truly demands it, and leave a comment explaining why.

Boring code ships faster, breaks less, and lets everyone go home on time. 🚀

**1/5**
Simple code beats clever code. Every time.

Clever code feels great to write. You get a small hit of pride when it works. But code is read far more often than it is written, and the reader is usually you in six months, tired and confused.

**2/5**
Clever code has a hidden cost: it makes the reader decode it before they can understand it.

Simple code reads like a sentence. Clever code reads like a puzzle. Puzzles are fun on weekends, not during an outage at 2am.

**3/5**
Bugs love clever code.

The more tricks you stack, the harder it is to see edge cases. Simple code has fewer places to hide. When something breaks, you can find it in minutes instead of hours.

**4/5**
Simple code is easier to change.

Requirements always shift. A plain function with a clear name can be edited safely by anyone on the team. A one-line masterpiece usually gets rewritten from scratch because nobody dares touch it.

**5/5**
A good test: could a new teammate understand this without asking you?

If not, simplify it. Use clear names, small functions, and obvious control flow. Save the cleverness for the problem you're solving, not for how you express the solution.
